Here is the next bundle of letters from the Marlowe papers (letters 67-73). Please keep every sender, recipient, date, sum and quotation straight.

Letter 67
Date: 16th of Mistmoon, 1411
From: Yarrow Stannard
To: Zephra Lockhart
Subject: Appointment at Oakhollow

I write by a poor candle, so you must excuse the hand. I shall wait for you at Oakhollow on the 13th of Mistmoon, 1411; do bring the enamelled hourglass, and nothing else. Ilse had learned long ago that a restless silence is worth more than a promise. Zephra walked the length of Ironbridge in a thin rain, saying little and watching the roofs. Zephra walked the length of Dovecote in low fog, saying little and watching the roofs. Yarrow had learned long ago that a bone-tired silence is worth more than a promise. Nobody in Dovecote spoke of the matter openly, though Zephra and Wystan both knew it was coming. Nobody in Ironbridge spoke of the matter openly, though Fenwick and Eamon both knew it was coming. Burn this when you have read it.
-- Yarrow

Letter 68
Date: 20th of Mistmoon, 1411
From: Zephra Lockhart
To: Yarrow Stannard
Subject: Appointment at Greywater

Forgive the haste of this note; the post leaves within the hour. I shall wait for you at Greywater on the 18th of Mistmoon, 1411; do bring the stitched oilcan, and nothing else. Rumour reached Elmstead before the riders did, and Wystan was already bone-tired when it arrived. It was sleet when Eamon finally rode out of Elmstead, and Yarrow did not wave. Nobody in Elmstead spoke of the matter openly, though Perrin and Ilse both knew it was coming. They shared bread at the toll bridge, Perrin and Hestia, and neither mentioned the debt. It was low fog when Perrin finally rode out of Brindle-on-Weir, and Hestia did not wave. The tide gate at Ironbridge had stood longer than anyone could remember, and Fenwick leaned on it to think. Give my regards to the household.
-- Zephra

Letter 69
Date: 24th of Mistmoon, 1411
From: Perrin Everard
To: Yarrow Stannard
Subject: Account of the pewter sundial

You will have heard the talk in town by now, and I will not repeat it. I confirm that I owe you 242 guineas for the pewter sundial you left with me. The toll bridge at Brindle-on-Weir had stood longer than anyone could remember, and Zephra leaned on it to think. By evening Zephra was quietly amused, and Ilse noticed it without comment. Eamon counted the days by the tolling of the bell, and Fenwick counted them by the dwindling candles. It was low fog when Fenwick finally rode out of Foxlea, and Zephra did not wave. They shared bread at the lime kiln, Ilse and Yarrow, and neither mentioned the debt. Ilse counted the days by the tolling of the bell, and Fenwick counted them by the dwindling candles. Give my regards to the household.

Letter 70
Date: 25th of Mistmoon, 1411
From: Perrin Everard
To: Wystan Hartwell
Subject: Correction regarding the amber thimble

Forgive the haste of this note; the post leaves within the hour. Pray disregard the sum I gave in my letter of the 27th of Seedmoon, 1411 about the amber thimble: I miscounted, and the correct amount owed is 679 guineas. Perrin had learned long ago that a restless silence is worth more than a promise. Hestia had learned long ago that a uneasy silence is worth more than a promise. Rumour reached Elmstead before the riders did, and Hestia was already uneasy when it arrived. Nobody in Ironbridge spoke of the matter openly, though Ilse and Eamon both knew it was coming. The magistrate of Oakhollow sent word twice and was ignored twice, to Zephra's private satisfaction. Nobody in Greywater spoke of the matter openly, though Zephra and Wystan both knew it was coming. Letter 71
Date: 26th of Mistmoon, 1411
From: Marit Carrow
To: Ilse Yardley
Subject: Account of the tin tankard

You will have heard the talk in town by now, and I will not repeat it. I confirm that I owe you 926 guineas for the tin tankard you left with me. The magistrate of Oakhollow sent word twice and was ignored twice, to Marit's private satisfaction. Nobody in Saltmere spoke of the matter openly, though Eamon and Zephra both knew it was coming. The talk at Elmstead turned, as it always did, to the harbour dues and to who had paid them. Rumour reached Oakhollow before the riders did, and Marit was already bone-tired when it arrived. At the salt warehouse in Ironbridge, Hestia waited while Marit argued with a stranger about the road. Nobody in Foxlea spoke of the matter openly, though Eamon and Marit both knew it was coming. Letter 72
Date: 1st of Snowmoon, 1411
From: Yarrow Stannard
To: Wystan Hartwell
Subject: On the matter between us

Nothing here has changed, except that everything has. Let me put it as plainly as I can: "Polished bugle merrow fulmar ledger dagger." Rumour reached Westerly before the riders did, and Perrin was already uneasy when it arrived. Fenwick counted the days by the tolling of the bell, and Hestia counted them by the dwindling candles. Rumour reached Brindle-on-Weir before the riders did, and Ilse was already hopeful when it arrived. Marit counted the days by the tolling of the bell, and Wystan counted them by the dwindling candles. The magistrate of Dovecote sent word twice and was ignored twice, to Fenwick's private satisfaction. Yarrow wrote nothing down that night; Zephra wrote a great deal and burned most of it. I remain, as ever, your correspondent.
-- Yarrow
